vignette:
Leila sits at her desk in the open-plan office, surrounded by the steady hum of servers and the click of keyboards. Her eyes move across the database logs on her screen, scanning for anomalies-a task she performs with a precision that her supervisor often praises. But Leila does not feel precise. Her chest is tight, her shoulders hunched. Every time a colleague laughs too loudly two cubicles away, her body flinches before her mind can catch up. She tells herself it's just an office. She tells herself she is safe. The telling does not help.

Eighteen months ago, Leila was not here. She was inside the logistics hub of a regional military base in her home country, a quiet reservist with a talent for spreadsheets. She had joined because her father believed it would give her discipline, and because university was delayed. She never expected to see combat. But one evening, during a routine supply inventory, mortar fire struck the compound. The blast threw her against a metal shelving unit. She remembers the screaming of the soldier beside her, the smell of diesel and blood, the way her hands shook as she tried to call for help on a radio that had no signal. She remembers waiting for hours, pressed behind overturned crates, certain that any moment would be her last.

Her physical wounds healed quickly. The military offered her counselling, but she declined. She wanted to forget. She told herself that others had suffered far worse. She left the service a few months later and moved to a different country for a civilian job in data management, hoping that numbers and logic would replace the chaos inside her head.

They have not.

Leila now avoids anything that reminds her of that night. She deleted her military photos, stopped speaking to old comrades, and chose an apartment with no windows in the bedroom-a decision she justified as better for sleeping. She cannot ride in elevators with strangers, because the enclosed space triggers a panicked restlessness that makes her want to claw at the walls. She always takes the stairs, even if that means climbing eight floors. At work, she positions her desk so her back is to a corner, and she monitors the door constantly. When a co-worker approaches from behind, her heart pounds and she resists the urge to spin around aggressively. She knows this reaction is extreme, but she cannot control it.

Her sleep is fractured. Two or three times a week she wakes in a cold sweat, the echo of mortar fire reverberating in her ears. In the dream, she is always still trapped behind the crates, and no one comes. Sometimes she does not sleep at all, spending the night reorganising her database documentation or watching security camera footage of the apartment lobby-anything to feel a semblance of vigilance. During the day, she cannot concentrate. She double-checks her own queries repeatedly, terrified that a single mistake will cause a system failure-an irrational fear she cannot shake. Her mood is brittle. She has stopped returning calls from her mother, who asks too many questions about her life. Leila feels numb, disconnected from everyone around her, as if a sheet of glass separates her from the world. She does not date. She does not laugh.

Recently, at her annual review, her manager noted that her performance was still excellent, but that she seemed "distracted." Leila smiled and promised to focus better. That night, she sat alone in her windowless room, staring at the database schema on her laptop screen, and felt the familiar tightness in her chest. She wanted to call someone. She did not know who to call. So she opened a new query window and began typing, because that-organising data, making sense of rows and columns-was the only thing she still felt she could control.
